INTRO1: Today's topic is Global Factors: five external factors that influence the world of business.
S1: Globalisation is the growing integration of our world. In business, it means that world economies depend more and more on each other.
Its main effects are the free movement of capital, goods and services, the development of international trade, and more multinational corporations.
Four key factors made it possible: transport, communication, labour in less developed countries, and free trade, promoted by the World Trade Organisation.
Supporters say that globalisation helps poorer countries to develop and raises living standards.
Opponents say that it increases inequality, helps the countries that are already rich, and hurts local businesses.
S2: Today we are living the Fourth Industrial Revolution, also called Industry four point zero.
Its main features are automation, artificial intelligence, smart factories and more skilled workers.
With the Internet of Things, machines have sensors and exchange data. A digital twin is a virtual copy of a process or a production line.
Artificial intelligence lets machines work without people, and machine learning lets them find patterns and improve.
Edge computing processes data on your own device. Cloud computing delivers services over the internet.
S3: Because of globalisation, technology and migration, different cultures and identities now live side by side.
Many people believe that everyone should have equal opportunities, whatever their gender, age, ethnicity, religion or ability.
Most young people looking for a job, Generation Z, think that a company's commitment to diversity and inclusion is important.
So, to attract and keep young talent, companies need to rethink their recruitment policies.
S4: Since twenty nineteen, the world has seen a wave of instability: a pandemic, political tensions and new conflicts.
During the pandemic, many factories closed, and there were shortages of workers and delays in supplies.
In Europe, Brexit brought new rules, customs problems and uncertainty for trade.
The war in Ukraine caused inflation, so transport costs and the prices of raw materials went up.
Some changes will probably stay, like virtual meetings, remote work and a more digital workplace.
S5: Climate change is a vital factor for business: ninety-seven per cent of organisations have already been affected.
It increases the risk of extreme weather, and new rules against pollution force companies to invest.
Customers prefer products made by companies that reduce their impact on the environment.
Some resources become scarce and more expensive, and the demand for some goods changes.
Working conditions can get worse, for example when people work outdoors in extreme heat.
GL1: Here are the key words of this lesson.
Interdependence: economies that depend on each other.
Free trade: promoted by the World Trade Organisation.
Economies of scale: the cost per item is lower for large quantities.
Least developed countries: the poorest countries in the world.
Smart factory: a plant that is more efficient, more productive and less wasteful.
Digital twin: a virtual copy of a process or a production line.
Shortage: when there is not enough of something, like workers or raw materials.
Recruitment: the way a company finds and hires new people.
RF1: Let's review the whole lesson: five global factors that influence business.
One: globalisation, the growing interdependence of world economies.
Two: technological advancement and Industry four point zero.
Three: diversity and inclusion, with equal opportunities for everyone.
Four: world instability, from the pandemic to Brexit and the war in Ukraine.
Five: environmental concerns, because climate change affects every business.
